cues.text: Welcome to MIT 8111, Ethics and Legal Issues in Information Technology.
This is Study Session 1, Data Privacy and Legal Frameworks, and the frameworks we will be working with are the GDPR, HIPAA, the NDPR and the NDPA.
We begin with the first chapter: privacy, security and ethics.
Let us start with the most basic question.
What is personal data?
Personal data is information relating to an identified or identifiable person.
Notice those two words, identified and identifiable.
A person is identified when you already know who they are.
A person is identifiable when you could work out who they are from the information, even if their name does not appear.
So personal data includes names, identifiers, location, transaction history and online identifiers, where those can be linked to a person.
That qualification, where linkable, matters.
An online identifier on its own may seem anonymous, but if it can be linked back to an individual, it counts.
Next, sensitive data.
Sensitive data may include health information, biometrics used to uniquely identify people, and other protected categories, depending on the law.
Pay attention to that last phrase, depending on the law.
Which categories count as protected is not identical everywhere, so you must always check the particular law that applies.
Now to three ideas that are often confused: privacy, security, and the relationship between them.
Privacy concerns whether collection, use, sharing, retention and control are appropriate.
In other words, privacy asks whether it is right for this data to be collected at all, how it is used, who it is shared with, how long it is kept, and what control the person has over it.
Security, by contrast, protects confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Confidentiality means only authorised people can access the data.
Integrity means the data is accurate and has not been improperly altered.
Availability means the data can be accessed when it is legitimately needed.
Here is the point that connects them.
A securely encrypted database can still violate privacy if its purpose is illegitimate.
Imagine a database that is perfectly protected against hackers, yet it was built to collect people's information for a purpose that is not legitimate.
The security is excellent, but the privacy violation remains.
Security is therefore necessary, but it is not sufficient.
Strong security does not make a purpose appropriate.
Now let us turn to law and ethics.
Law defines enforceable obligations.
If you breach a legal obligation, there can be consequences imposed through legal processes.
Ethics asks a different question: what conduct is justified, including beyond the legal minimum.
So the law sets a floor, and ethics invites us to ask whether we should do more than the floor requires.
Something can be lawful and still be questionable ethically.
Then there is compliance.
Compliance is demonstrated adherence to applicable obligations, not merely possession of a policy.
Having a privacy policy written down is not enough.
An organisation must be able to show that it actually follows the obligations that apply to it.
This leads to accountability, which requires evidence.
If you claim you comply, you must be able to prove it.
Finally, let us fix the key roles, because you will meet them repeatedly in every framework we study.
A data controller determines purposes and means.
That is, the controller decides why the data is processed and how.
A processor acts on behalf of a controller, carrying out processing for the controller rather than deciding the purposes itself.
The data subject is the individual concerned, the person the data is about.
One last subtlety.
A vendor may be a processor for some activities and a controller for others.
The role is not fixed by the type of organisation or by the label on a contract.
It depends on the activity.
For one activity, the vendor may act on behalf of a customer, and so be a processor.
For another, the same vendor may decide the purposes and means itself, and so be a controller.
When you analyse any scenario, ask of each activity: who determines the purposes and means?
To bring the chapter together: personal data is information about identified or identifiable people.
Privacy asks whether handling is appropriate, while security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability.

Law sets enforceable obligations, ethics reaches beyond them, compliance must be demonstrated, accountability requires evidence, and the roles of controller, processor and data subject depend on who decides purposes and means.
